title: Indentured Labour: How Britain Replaced Slavery With 2 MILLION Indians

cliffs.text: Everyone knows the British Empire abolished slavery in 1833. But almost no one knows about the system they built 3 years later to replace it. The British Empire used people from India to run this new system involving somewhere between 20 to 30 lakh Indians. Recruiters lied to them in their villages. Ships carried them across the oceans and on the plantations, the survivors called it slavery with chains taken off. This is the story India almost forgot.

blocks.text: Everyone knows the British Empire abolished slavery in 1833. But almost no one knows about the system they built 3 years later to replace it. The British Empire used people from India to run this new system involving somewhere between 20 to 30 lakh Indians. Recruiters lied to them in their villages. Ships carried them across the oceans and on the plantations, the survivors called it slavery with chains taken off. This is the story India almost forgot.

>> India might actually be a kind of replacement for Africa. India and Indians are answer to the labor void >>  >> that had opened up in the old slave colonies. They were called the Gladstone Coolies after the Anglo-Indian  word for manual labor. >> January 1836. A slave owner named John Gladstone sits at his desk in England. He owns massive sugar plantations in the Caribbean, but he has a major problem. 3

years ago, British Empire banned slavery. His workers are about to walk free and he has no plans to pay them real wages. So, he writes a letter to a shipping company in Calcutta. He asks a simple question, "Can you send me 100 Indians on a contract for 5 years?" The reply was yes. 2 years later, ships landed in the Caribbean carrying the first wave of Indian men. Over the next 80 years, lakhs of Indians followed them and one of those people, five generations later,

has a great-grandson living in Toronto today. >> My name is Shawn Binda. I'm the host of Hindu Lifestyle. My parents are from the island of Trinidad and Tobago and my great-great-grandfather came from India and we are part of the indentured laborers that {quote} unquote left India and they went to the island of Trinidad. >> To understand how millions of Indians ended up on those ships, you have to look at the villages they left behind. The 1830s were a very terrible time for

India. The British had been running the country for decades. The fields that used to grow food were now forced to grow opium and indigo for the empire. Local industries were dying. Famines were striking places like Bengal and Madras Presidency over and over again. This is the desperate world the recruiters walked into. Locals called them Arkaties. In Bhojpuri language, that word came to mean kidnapper. These recruiters hung around busy pilgrimage sites, river crossings, and village

wells during famine years. Wherever desperate people gathered, they were waiting. They even told people they could come home for the weekend from a country across an ocean they had never seen. They also knew exactly who to target. Widows, runaway wives, poor laborers who didn't own any land. They looked for people the village wouldn't go searching for. Female recruiters listened to gossip at village wells, pick up secrets, and use them to trap women into signing. When the contract finally appeared, it was written entirely in English. The craziest part

is the person signing it couldn't read a single word. >> First Indians that left were in the 1830s or so, so they first went to Mauritius and then in the Caribbean the first boat that arrived was in Guyana in 1838. When this indentureship came up, they were sold a bag of riches that actually never really panned out. >> If you walked onto one of those ships, you were stepping into a ghost story. The very ships carrying these new workers were often exact same wooden vessels that carried enslaved Africans

10 years earlier. They sailed exact same routes. The British Empire didn't retire the ships when they banned slavery. They just changed the labels on the cargo. The slave trade's journey across the ocean was a horrific crime that killed about 12% of its captives. But for Indian women and children on these new legal voyages, the journey was far more deadlier. Look at the numbers from just one route in Trinidad. Over half of all babies died before seeing land. More

than third of young girls perished. Nearly one in five women never survived the trip. Why were there so many women on board? It wasn't to protect them, and it wasn't to keep families together. The British Empire had a strict rule. For every 100 men they shipped, they had to send 40 women. The excuse? They believed having women around would keep men calm and easy to control. This meant single women fleeing hard lives at homes were trapped on floating prison for four months completely at the mercy of ship's crew and 100 desperate strangers. But in

the middle of that pitch darkness, the system broke. These people boarded the ship as complete strangers. Back in India, they were divided by different languages and strict caste rules. They were people who would never have shared a cup of water, but suddenly they were crammed together sharing small plates of rice on a violently swaying deck. They chose  to do something incredible. They looked at the survivors next to them and threw away old rules. They decided to become family. They called each other Jahaji Bhai. They put strangers in a hold of slave ship, but

those strangers came out as a unified brotherhood. When they finally stepped onto dry land, they quickly realized they weren't free at all. In fact, the British had built a legal trap. >> The British Empire, they needed people to look after sugar, cotton. The Indians were known for their agricultural expertise. So they So they took them and they brought them to the Caribbean to to look after all of In Guyana and Trinidad in particular. They had the sugar estates that that a lot of people worked

on. >> They didn't needed a heavy iron chains to control you anymore. They had something much more effective, the courtroom. If you walk one foot off the plantation without a physical pass, you were a criminal. If you refused a task because your body was failing, you were a criminal. If you got sick on the wrong day, you were a criminal. The trap worked perfectly. More than one in five indentured laborers ended up convicted of a crime. They took a simple Tamil word, [ __ ] which meant wages or a job description. But the British Empire took the word and twisted it. They turned it

into a deeply painful racial slur, similar to N-word. Once the government branded you with it, you could never wash it off. Your grandson could be a successful lawyer in Trinidad in 1950 and the local newspapers would still call him a [ __ ] On the sugar plantations, there was a strict hierarchy. Indians were placed at the very bottom. They were below the English, the Scottish, Irish, and the African descendants of former slaves. Who were sometimes made overseers. Every single group above you held power over you. The Indians move into their old

cabins. >> Their old living places of the former slaves. Or they're provided with similar in a similar location. I mean, one particular plantation that I know in the middle of Jamaica to this day has on the edge of its sugar fields an area called India. >> The same dirt floors, the same walls, no privacy, no toilets, and no clean drinking water. In their folk songs, the workers compared to barracks to stables or used the word narak, which means hell.

>> White man I shoot. I no go this side. I no go that side. So, me belong to no friend me and them. Kana kana them. Our people own, watch our own. good details. >> Historians call this a new form of slavery because the outcome was exactly the same. The British simply replaced the whip with courtroom, bringing people over in massive targeted numbers. >> In the Caribbean in particular, there was about 400,000 that actually came. By By most accounts, when when you try to trace this back, anywhere between 80 to

85% of the indentured laborers were Hindu. 10 to 12% were Muslim. But due to the colonial influence, there was a good portion that did convert to Christianity afterwards as well. >> Most of these families were Hindu and they tried their best to keep their faith alive. But the colonial government made it illegal to practice their religion in public. This started with how they treated their dead. >> One of the things that we know as  as Hindus is that we cremate the

dead. And in Trinidad in particular, this was not recognized by the state. And a lot of times what Hindus family did is that they went to the fields and they did this practice in private,  in secret. And when finally they made the push to to have cremation recognized, the first site of cremation was a garbage dump in Trinidad. >> The exact same thing happened to the weddings. For decades, the government refused to recognize Hindu marriages. >> If you go into a Caribbean family's home

and you look at photos of wedding ceremonies from the '60s and and the '70s, you would typically see they would have photos of the bride and the groom in their Indian attire. But then they would have a separate photo where they're wearing on the white wedding dress and the suit. They would do the Hindu ceremony, then they would go to either the government offices and they would register saying that yes, we were married under your state laws. >> Over time, they built schools. The Prime Minister of Trinidad once mocked these buildings as cow sheds. Yet, those cow

sheds produced world-class lawyers, doctors, and eventually prime ministers. Today, this history has created a beautiful, resilient culture across the Caribbean. >> No matter how Hinduism has evolved outside is that if you talk to any of the West Indians, they always viewed Bharat as that ancestral homeland. And while they're not might be a current connection to India as the state, but that view that India that Bharat as the motherland is always there. >> The empire kept its strict paperwork,
but the survivors kept their bhajans to endure and survive. This is a story of forgotten indentured laborers.
